div.head: 382. Memorandum of Conversation

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: Secretary’s Meeting with Ecuadorean President Leon Febres-Cordero

div.p: President Febres-Cordero made an insistent appeal for additional U.S. assistance in his meeting with the Secretary. He emphasized the social costs which his economic rationalization policies have entailed. Febres-Cordero said more U.S. aid would help him convince the Ecuadorean people that the temporary sacrifices he has asked them to bear will pay off. He asserted that he could not carry out his program without additional U.S. help. Febres-Cordero specifically mentioned PL–480, ESF, oil sales, and a multi-year Paris Club rescheduling agreement. The Secretary promised to look into how the U.S. might be able to increase assistance after he returns to Washington. END SUMMARY.

The Secretary stopped at the military portion of Guayaquil Airport for three hours on February 28 for a bilateral and lunch hosted by President Leon Febres-Cordero. The initial bilateral lasted almost 40 minutes.

The Secretary told President Febres-Cordero that he directed much of his time to arms control and the Middle East. Jordan, Egypt, and Iraq are responding to our concern that they
come forward and actively seek progress toward peace. But President Reagan wishes to give primary foreign policy attention to our own neighborhood. We recognize that Febres-Cordero and we are on the same wavelength, and we appreciate that he is a democratically-elected president.

Febres-Cordero responded that his policies, both foreign and domestic, were coherent. He had done in his seven months in office exactly what he had said he would do. His policies were designed to support democracy and free enterprise—not only in Ecuador, but as a model for all South America. He had told us in June when he had met with the President, the Vice-President, and the Secretary that he needed our assistance. On taking office, he discovered that the economic situation of the country was worse than he had believed. He said he now needed our help desperately.

Febres-Cordero said he had to state very candidly, however, that so far he had received only sympathy rather than action. The aid he expected, which he thought he had a right to expect in view of his effort to promote shared policies and values, had not come. His policies were not conditioned on U.S. assistance, but we should understand that he lacked the resources to succeed on his own and that he was isolated from the rest of South America. He was thus shocked to get a report from the Foreign Ministry that for FY 1986, Ecuador was absolutely at the bottom of the list of U.S. aid recipients in Latin America.

Febres-Cordero said he hoped to make the Secretary understand that what was at stake was the stability of democracy in Ecuador. It will take time for his economic stabilization measures and encouragement of private enterprise to show results. In the meantime, he needed resources to convince the people that the current sacrifices will lead to greater well-being. Febres-Cordero noted that the U.S. would need oil for its strategic petroleum reserve. He hoped Ecuador could supply some reasonable portion, such as 40,000 BPD, to stabilize its production and income.

The Secretary said it might be useful if we reviewed each type of aid to see what could be done, although he didn’t have all the numbers in his head. The Secretary recalled that Febres-Cordero and he had discussed a housing program last May. Febres-Cordero said that program seemed to be working well up until now, but that he understood that the Treasury Department had opposed a Housing Guarantee program beyond FY 1985. The Secretary explained that we are well-off as a country, but that President Reagan was concerned about reducing our budget deficit. Subsidies were being reduced in several areas,
including housing, but so far as he knew our assistance to the Ecuadorean housing program was going forward. The Secretary said he would be glad to push for more help in Washington, but the Ecuadoreans had to single out particular areas and programs, rather than simply asking for more assistance in general.

Febres-Cordero responded that he had requested $25 million in PL–480, but we had agreed to only $15 million. The extra $10 million in assistance would make a tremendous difference to the growth of the agricultural sector. Furthermore, the GOE had agreed with the steering committee of the private banks on a multi-year rescheduling of official debts, but it would need our help in negotiating a similar arrangement with official creditors in the Paris Club. The Secretary agreed to look into both these matters, though he noted that questions of precedent and comparability would have to be considered in the Paris Club.

The Secretary returned to the question of PL–480, asking if ten million more in FY 1985 would satisfy the Ecuadoreans. Febres-Cordero said yes; Ambassador Hart noted that negotiations were set to begin on the $15 million that had been approved for FY 1985. Febres-Cordero noted that the USG was proposing $15 million in ESF for Ecuador in FY 1986 and asked that Ecuador receive at least that much. He tied his need for short term assistance to next January’s congressional elections, which he said would amount to a verdict on his entire administration and policy orientation. The Secretary again agreed to look into Febres-Cordero’s request on his return to Washington.

The President asserted that he has had to make extraordinary efforts himself, indeed to go beyond the limits of Ecuador’s obsolete drug laws, to make progress in the fight against illicit drug trafficking. The effort has been perhaps the most successful of all his Government’s initiatives, precisely because the U.S. had responded to Ecuador’s request for assistance in fighting drug traffickers. This kind of cooperation and mutual effort should be replicated in other areas. The Secretary expressed appreciation for the GOE’s interdiction efforts and noted that it was in Ecuador’s own interests to prevent the drug traffickers from getting out of control as they had in Colombia.

The Secretary agreed with Febres-Cordero’s emphasis on making a market economy work. But he told Febres-Cordero that Ecuador’s economy seemed to be doing better than the President was giving himself credit for. The Secretary praised the President’s prudent prediction of two and a half percent real growth in 1985, in spite of optimistic predictions of over four percent growth by some of his advisers. Better to predict two or three percent and achieve four percent than vice versa. The Secretary further noted that the U.S. must take into account economic performance in deciding how much help a country needed when allocating its assistance to various aid recipients.

Febres-Cordero rejoined that political concurrence among aid donors and recipients also should be considered. Moreover, he faced an unprecedented alliance between bitterly divided Moscow-line and Maoist-line communists. It was precisely his strong preference for a free market policy which had overcome the communists’ strong internal rivalries. He also faced intervention from Nicaragua, the Soviet Union, and other Communist countries, but he could handle their subversive activities. What he could not handle was a popular reaction to his economic rationalization measures during a transition to a thriving free market economy. The Secretary reiterated his willingness to push for more help for Ecuador on his return to Washington. The initial meeting then turned into a smaller bilateral, with only the President, the Secretary, the Foreign Minister, and Assistant Secretary Motley remaining.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 51E, Ecuador. Confidential. Drafted in the Embassy in Ecuador; cleared by Motley and McKinley and PA, OAS, and S. The meeting took place in the Guayaquil airport. Shultz visited Guayaquil on February 28 before travelling to Montevideo for Sanguinetti’s inauguration, March 1–2.

In telegram 11483 from Quito, December 18, 1984, Hart wrote: “President Febres-Cordero vented his frustrations to me on December 16 about what he considers to be inadequate U.S. financial support for his government. I set the record straight by citing our extensive economic assistance, but I doubt he was convinced.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N840015–0003)

Shultz sent a March 15 letter to Secretary of Energy John Herrington requesting Department of Energy cooperation in “arranging a joint Department of Energy/Defense Fuel Supply Center team to visit Quito, Ecuador, to discuss SPR procurement procedures with the Febres-Cordero government.” (Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 51E, Ecuador) In an April 5 memorandum to Shultz, Motley noted that the Department of Energy “plans no further purchases of sour crude, the only type Ecuador has to offer for the remainder of FY85.” Furthermore, given the probability of an SPR purchase moratorium in FY86, Motley recommended that no joint team be sent to Ecuador. Shultz approved the recommendation. (Ibid)
No memorandum of conversation for a May meeting between Shultz and Febres-Cordero has been found. See footnote 4, Document 379.
